claims.statement: Tom Allen opened a saloon in 1868 at the present home of the Boatmen's bank (printed as 'fan'), at Fourth Street and Washington Avenue.
Tom Allen was a tenant of the real estate firm J. C. Kaime & Bro. ever since he opened his saloon.
Tom Allen opened a saloon near the present home of the Boatmen's Bank, at Fourth Street and Washington Avenue, in 1868.
Tom Allen was busy superintending the opening of his new saloon on Fitch street, St. Louis (printed as 'Fitch stzee}', street name garbled).
The last $800 of stakes for the Allen and McCoole fight was put up at Tom Allen's saloon, with a large crowd present.
Tom Allen attended to business as a boniface (innkeeper) in St. Louis until 10 May 1869.
Tom Allen's saloon was on Fifth Street near Biddle (printed as 'Filth' and 'Bid-die').
Tom Allen's Concert Saloon on Fifth Street, between O'Fallon and Biddle, was almost uncomfortably full on the night of 14 June 1869, a 'Free and Easy' night.
A photograph of Tom Allen hung over the array of decanters in his concert saloon.
After the referee's decision, a crowd went to Tom Allen's saloon and the Concert Saloon was liberally patronized.
Tom Allen owned a saloon in June 1869, which the paper urged him to dispose of.
Tom Allen wrote to a St. Louis friend that he would buy Gallagher's business at a fair valuation and buy out other champions who wished to sell.
$100 was deposited for a match at the Wash Home or at Tom Allen's saloon on Fifth street.
Tom Allen and Jim Coyne invited their friends to Allen's saloon on Fifth street that evening.
Tom Allen was in town last night at his saloon on Fifth street, in first-rate condition.
The final stakes for the fight between Tom Allen and Charley Gallagher were deposited at Allen's saloon on the night of August 14, 1869.
Tom Allen was to be at his saloon on Saturday night with his trainer Jim Coyne, where the public and his friends could see him.
On the night of 14 August 1869 a crowd packed Allen's saloon while the battle money was deposited.
On the night of 14 August 1869 a crowd packed Allen's saloon while the battle money was deposited.
Tom Allen's saloon, a 'Concert Saloon' on Fifth Street between Biddle and O'Fallon streets, had a bar in front and a back room with tables and a piano.
Tom Allen's saloon was at 1205 Fifth Street, St. Louis, in October 1869.
The stakes were put up at Allen's saloon before a large crowd, with Allen and Jim Coyne said to be present.
Jim Coyne held a levee at Tom Allen's saloon in St. Louis on 1 November 1869 and was welcomed by many friends.
After retiring, Tom Allen opened a saloon on Market Street near Seventh.
Tom Allen hosted a presentation of colors at his saloon to George Seddons of Boston.
John C. Heenan and James Mace visited Tom Allen's concert room on Washington avenue in St. Louis.
Deposits for a match between George Seddons and Johnny Lafferty were to be made at Tom Allen's saloon in St. Louis.
J. L. Hughes, a Californian, left a $500 forfeit to be found at Tom Allen's saloon for a challenge to fight at light weight.
Tom Allen invited his friends to a free and easy evening at his place, No. 417 Washington avenue, on July 16, 1870.
A $100-a-side fight between Punch Morris and Steve O'Donnell was made up at Tom Allen's saloon on Saturday night.
The forfeit money for the Morris and O'Donnell fight was put up at Tom Allen's saloon.
John Madden said terms for a match with Buckey Barrett could be arranged by calling at Tom Allen's saloon.
Collins, the Cast Iron Man, wrote that he would be ready at a St. Louis saloon to put up $50 to $100 to meet Annabury.
Collins invited Mr. Annabury's friends to make arrangements at Tom Allen's saloon on Saturday evening, August 20, 1870.
The last preliminary deposit for the Allen and Gallagher fight was made at Allen's saloon, with John Campbell holding the stakes.
The last instalment of battle money was put up at Allen's saloon, with Roach putting up $200 for Allen and Kelly $100 for Gallagher.
J. C. Gallagher visited Tom Allen at his saloon on Washington avenue on November 2, 1870.
Tom Allen planned a grand opening of his new concert hall at 417 Washington avenue on Saturday, March 4, 1871, with concerts every Saturday, Sunday and Monday evening.
Jem Mace was to be Tom Allen's guest for three or four days before leaving for Kansas City to meet Joe Coburn.
Jem Mace made Tom Allen's saloon in St. Louis his favorite resort while training for the Coburn match.
Tom Allen's Free Concert Hall was open on Saturday, Sunday, Monday and Wednesday evenings.
Tom Allen had a concert saloon at 417 Washington avenue.
Tom Allen and Jem Mace were to meet their friends at Allen's free-and-easy at the saloon that night.
Dispatches from the Mace-Coburn fight were to be received at Tom Allen's saloon at 417 Washington avenue (printed as 417 Wesbicg on avenve).
A reporter interviewed Tom Allen at his popular Washington avenue resort.
Tom Allen's saloon was at 417 Washington avenue, near Fifth street.
Tom Allen's saloon was on Washington avenue, between Fourth and Fifth streets, and the third deposit was made there.
At the time of his 1873 fight with McCoole, Tom Allen kept a saloon on Washington Avenue between Fourth and Fifth streets, St. Louis.
Tom Allen's saloon was crowded with fight followers on the evening of 22 September 1873.
Tom Allen's free-and-easy on Washington avenue was crowded on the evening of 22 September 1873.
That night Tom Allen made a speech at his saloon, telling the crowd to take a walk.
Tom Allen presided over his Saturday night 'free and racy' on 1873-10-04; the paper does not name the place.
An advertisement says Tom Allen's Free Concert Hall at 417 Washington Avenue is open every evening, with the champion presiding.
An advertisement says Tom Allen's Free Concert Hall at 417 Washington Avenue is the best place of amusement in the city, open every evening with the champion presiding.
Betting at Tom Allen's Washington Avenue saloon the night before the fight made him the strong favorite.
A Democrat reporter found Tom Allen in the back room of Allen's Saloon while asking for sporting news.
